blocks.text: INT4 quantization represents weights using 4-bit integers with uniformly spaced levels, the deployment focused counterpart to the NF4 format covered in the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module, which was specifically designed around the distribution of neural network weights rather than a simple even spacing.

This topic draws a direct comparison between INT4 and NF4, clarifying when each format fits better, and sets up the GPTQ and AWQ topics later in this module, both of which commonly produce INT4 style quantized output.
1. What INT4 Quantization Means

blocks.alt: A floating point weight gets converted into an INT4 integer weight

blocks.text: INT4 quantization maps floating point weight values onto 16 discrete integer levels, the same total count as NF4 covered in the earlier module, but using plain, evenly spaced integer levels rather than NF4 distribution aware placement.
2. INT4 vs the NF4 Format Covered Earlier

blocks.alt: NF4 uses distribution aware levels while INT4 uses uniform levels

blocks.text: Where NF4, covered in depth in the earlier NF4 Quantization topic, places more of its 16 levels near zero to match how real neural network weights actually cluster, INT4 spaces its 16 levels evenly across the representable range, a simpler but generally less precise approach for the same total number of levels.

blocks.text: 3. Uniform Integer Levels vs Distribution Aware Levels

blocks.alt: Uniform spacing across the range produces 16 evenly spaced levels

blocks.text: The evenly spaced nature of INT4 levels makes it simpler to implement and reason about than NF4 distribution aware approach, though it means some representable levels get wasted on rarely occurring extreme values, the same fundamental limitation the earlier NF4 topic identified with naive uniform 4-bit quantization.

# A conceptual illustration of INT4's uniform level spacing
int4_levels = evenly_spaced(min_value, max_value, count=16)
# Compare to NF4, which concentrates levels near zero instead

blocks.text: 4. INT4 Memory Savings

blocks.alt: FP32 shrinks down to INT4, an eighth the memory

blocks.text: INT4 delivers the same dramatic eightfold memory reduction from full FP32 precision that the earlier 4-Bit Quantization topic covered, since both formats use the same total number of bits per weight, the difference lies entirely in how those bits get allocated across the representable range.
5. Quality Tradeoffs at 4-Bit Integer Precision

blocks.alt: INT4 having only 16 levels carries a more noticeable quality loss risk

blocks.text: Because INT4 uniform spacing does not account for how real weights actually distribute, it can introduce more noticeable quality degradation than NF4 for the same 16 level budget, which is exactly why more sophisticated algorithms like GPTQ and AWQ, covered in the next two topics, were developed to squeeze better quality out of this same 4-bit budget.

blocks.title: This directly motivates the next two topics in this module
blocks.content: GPTQ and AWQ both aim to improve on naive INT4 quantization quality through smarter calibration and weight importance analysis, worth keeping this quality gap in mind as those techniques get introduced.

blocks.text: 6. INT4 and Specialized Quantization Algorithms

blocks.alt: GPTQ and AWQ algorithms often produce INT4 style output

blocks.text: Rather than applying naive uniform INT4 quantization directly, most practical INT4 deployments today rely on more sophisticated algorithms like GPTQ or AWQ, covered in the next two topics of this module, which produce INT4 precision output but through a much smarter, calibration driven process than simple even spacing.
7. INT4 for Inference vs Training

blocks.alt: INT4 is deployment focused while NF4 via QLoRA is training focused

blocks.text: INT4, and the GPTQ and AWQ algorithms that commonly produce it, are primarily used for deployment and inference efficiency, while NF4 through QLoRA, covered in the earlier module, is specifically designed for the different challenge of fitting a training run in memory, the same training versus deployment distinction introduced in the earlier What Is Quantization topic.
8. Hardware Considerations for INT4

INT4 hardware support is generally narrower than INT8, covered in the previous topic, since 4-bit computation is a more specialized capability, worth checking specifically for a target deployment platform before committing to INT4 quantization for a production system.
9. Choosing Between INT4 and NF4

The choice between INT4 and NF4 largely comes down to context, NF4 for training time quantization within a QLoRA workflow, covered in the earlier module, and INT4, typically through a more sophisticated algorithm like GPTQ or AWQ, for deployment time quantization of an already fine-tuned model.
Worked Example
A team that fine-tuned a model using QLoRA, with its NF4 base model quantization covered in the earlier module, now wants to deploy that finished model as efficiently as possible for inference.

Rather than reusing the NF4 approach that served their training needs well, they apply GPTQ, covered in the next topic, to produce an INT4 quantized deployment version, recognizing that NF4 and plain INT4 quantization each serve their own distinct stage of the model lifecycle, and that a smarter algorithm like GPTQ improves on naive INT4 quality considerably.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming INT4 and NF4 are interchangeable, when their level placement strategies genuinely differ
Applying naive, evenly spaced INT4 quantization when a smarter algorithm like GPTQ or AWQ would preserve more quality at the same bit budget
Reusing training time NF4 quantization directly for a deployment scenario without considering deployment specific tools
Not checking hardware support for INT4 acceleration before assuming a deployment platform will benefit from it

blocks.text: Practice

In your own words, explain why NF4 distribution aware level placement generally preserves more model quality than plain INT4 uniform level placement, even though both formats use the same total number of bits per weight.
Key Takeaway

INT4 quantization uses 16 uniformly spaced integer levels, delivering the same eightfold memory reduction as NF4 but with generally lower quality due to its simpler, non distribution aware level placement, making it the more common deployment time format, typically produced through a smarter algorithm like GPTQ or AWQ rather than naive uniform quantization alone.
